newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Deutsche Bank has strong income gain.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Deutsche Bank has strong income gain.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG Wednesday reported a bigger-than-expected 27.5 percent jump in net income for the first half of 1997, sending its stock surging more than 5 percent.
This year's rally in financial markets enabled the bank to chalk up strong gains in trading and commission income, which offset the negative impact of the weak mark on its costs.
Net income rose to 1.5 billion marks ($823.8 million) from 1.2 billion ($656 million), beating analysts' forecasts, which had averaged 1.36 billion marks ($744 million).

Earnings were driven by trading income, which jumped 48.3 percent rise to 2.0 billion marks ($1.1 billion), and by group net commission income, which rose 25.7 percent to 4.1 billion marks ($2.2 billion).

A smiling Rolf Breuer told his first news briefing as chief executive that Deutsche was so well-positioned in its securities and asset management businesses that it was able to profit strongly from the rally in financial markets this year.
"It has rained porridge in the markets this year and we had the right spoon," he said.
The expansion of Deutsche's London-based investment banking business, though costly, had been an "overwhelming success" which was now bearing fruit, he said.

The news sent Deutsche's shares surging 5.3 percent to an all-time high of 127.50 marks in early bourse trade amid keen investor interest in a sector brimming with merger speculation following Monday's announcement of a megamerger between Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG (Hypo-Bank).

"It's a very good result. The figures were above expectations," said Christine Winkler, banking analyst at Bayerische Hypo-Bank. She said she would probably raise her earnings forecast for the full year.
Earnings per share rose 26.1 percent to 2.90 marks from 2.30 marks.

Risk provisions fell 35.3 percent to 500 million marks ($273 million) from 800 million marks ($437 million), reflecting that corporate insolvencies are likely to have peaked. Also, last year's risk provisions were boosted by funds set aside for engineering group KHD AG, which Deutsche helped bail out.

Analysts had expected a sharp rise in costs as the weakness of the mark against the British pound and the dollar made it more expensive for Deutsche to maintain and expand its London-based investment banking business.
